doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The army band's jazz combo and the records they heard
summary: His combo with William Boone played for the troops, and the men heard Monk, Bird, Diz and Miles records.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: There were good musicians, yeah. We had a jazz combo in the army band, in the 7th Division Band. We had the marching band, we had about a 14- to 15-piece dance band, and we had a jazz combo. In this jazz combo there was pianist named William Boone, who was a native of Brooklyn. If it hadn’t been for him I would have just gone completely out, because there was hardly anyone else to play with.
You mean at your level of ideas?

Yes, at my level certainly. I’ll agree with that. There were several musicians who wanted to, but they just couldn’t hang with us [laughs]. We had a bassist named James Legrange. He was from Cleveland. And a drummer named -- if I can think of his son. His son is a well-known trumpeter. He’s from Indianapolis. Whitted. Farris Pharez Whitted is the trumpet player, a young trumpeter. His father was the drummer in my --

We played a lot of engagements, mostly for other enlisted men in the army, officers. The band played for new recruits coming in. We play formations when another general came to review our outfit, a visiting officer from another outfit or something. We played a ceremony.
I’m curious. Were you getting records? Did people send you records? What were guys listening to?
We were listening to -- somebody had a record by Thelonious Monk. I heard Three in One, Straight, No Chaser, for the first time. And we had some Bird records and Diz records and Miles records.
So did you feel that you were getting enough to feel that you were still contemporary?
Yes, I wasn’t worried about losing that aspect. I was just worried about losing my life over there.
